newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall below key jobs data, dollar rallies.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall below key jobs data, dollar rallies.

text.p: Stocks and bonds moved lower Thursday as Wall Street braced for Friday's key U.S. jobs report for February, and as a source close to the Federal Reserve suggested the central bank might raise interest rates soon.
The dollar rallied to a three-year high against the German mark on robust U.S. economic data.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 1.15 points at 6,944.70. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,253 to 1,205 on active volume of 522 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It's amazing the Dow wasn't down more," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney. "You just didn't have any buyers today because you've got the moment of truth of the week tomorrow."

The cautious mood contrasted with Wednesday's session, when soothing comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan eased investors' fears that the central bank was planning some action to slow the stock market's rise and set off a rally of 93 points in the blue-chip Dow index.

But there was no exuberance in the market Thursday as investors braced for the possibility that a strong set of economic figures on Friday could prompt the Fed to pull the trigger on an interest rate increase.
"The stock market is struggling to get a true sense of the strength of the economy and what will be the course of Fed policy," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates.
The bond market was also on guard prior to the jobs data. The key 30-year Treasury bond lost 22/32, sending its yield up to 6.88 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.83 percent.

According to economists surveyed by Reuters, the report is expected to show 230,000 new jobs were created in February, down from 271,000 in January, and the nation's unemployment rate is expected to edge down to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.
Analysts said the market will look closely at the average hourly wage component of the report, which is seen rising by 0.4 percent from 0.1 percent a month ago.
The dollar rose to 1.7160 marks in late trading from 1.7127 late Wednesday. It fell to 121.08 Japanese yen from 121.15 yen.
Coffee prices suffered a setback following their recent rapid advance but soybeans powered to the highest level in 5-1/2 months.
Coffee prices spiraled sharply lower toward the end of the day on profit-taking one day after the market surged to its highest level in nearly 2-1/2 years.
May coffee futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange closed off 6.95 cents per pound at 193.70 cents.
Soybean futures closed sharply higher boosted by strong U.S. export sales and reports a leading analytical firm had cut its estimate for U.S. ending stocks for the 1996/97 year ending Aug. 31.
March futures on the Chicago Board of Trade closed 16-3/4 cents a bushel up at $8.18, just below an earlier 5-1/2 month high for the nearby contract of $8.18-1/2.
In New York, heating oil futures shook off their end-of-the-winter blues and settled with sharp gains.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, April heating oil ended up 0.89 cent at 53.43 cents a gallon. April gasoline ended up 1.15 cents a gallon at 64.48 cents.
April crude oil finished 45 cents higher at $20.94 a barrel.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed 39.2 points higher at 4,399.3. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei closed down 232.18 points, or 1.27 percent, at 18,041.33.
